t: Egg Drop With 2 Eggs and N Floors — Covering Floors with Fewest Drops
o: We must determine f — the highest floor from which an egg survives, anywhere in 0..n — using two identical eggs, where a broken egg is gone and every drop counts as a move, minimizing the worst case. The asymmetry drives everything: while both eggs are alive you may probe boldly, but once one breaks you must linear-scan upward from the lowest unknown floor. Example 1: n = 2 needs 2 moves — drop at floor 1, then floor 2 if it survived. Example 2: n = 100 answers 14 with a shrinking-gap schedule for the first egg (14, 27, 39, ...): a break at any point still leaves a scan that fits the same budget because 14 + 13 + ... + 1 = 105 covers all 100 floors, while 13 + 12 + ... + 1 = 91 does not.
k: One egg remaining forces a bottom-up linear scan — that asymmetry shapes the entire strategy.
If m moves remain, the first jump can span m floors; each survival shrinks the next jump by one, so m moves cover m(m+1)/2 floors in the worst case.
Answering the minimum is equivalent to finding the smallest m with m(m+1)/2 >= n.

a.i: Let dp[i] be the answer for i floors. Try dropping the first egg from every floor x of i: if it breaks, the x-1 floors below need a one-egg linear scan costing x-1 more moves; if it survives, dp[i-x] applies. The worst case is 1 + max(x-1, dp[i-x]) and we minimize over x. Quadratic but completely transparent — the natural interview starting point.
s: Set dp[0] = 0 and fill dp[i] for i = 1..n.
For each i try every first-drop floor x in 1..i.
Candidate cost is 1 + max(x - 1, dp[i - x]); keep the minimum.
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n floor counts, n candidate first-drop floors.

a.i: Invert the question: how many floors can m moves distinguish? Jump the surviving first egg m, then m-1, then m-2, ... so any break leaves exactly enough linear scans to finish within the same budget; total coverage is the triangular number m(m+1)/2. Scan m upward until coverage reaches n. Because m grows like sqrt(2n), this is dramatically faster than the DP and reduces to a closed form.
s: While covered < n, increment m and add m to covered.
a.t: O(sqrt(n)) — m reaches roughly sqrt(2n) before the triangular sum covers n.

w: Open with the DP to show systematic reasoning, then land the triangular-number inversion as the punchline. Pitfalls: forgetting f ranges over 0..n (n+1 outcomes, absorbed naturally by the coverage inequality), and reaching for binary search on the building — with one egg left you cannot binary-search anything. Follow-up: the classic k-egg version (LC 887), where the same coverage argument plus binary search over moves solves it in O(k log n).
